items.title: Human Rights & the NHRC framework
items.body:
## Human rights in India

- **Human rights** = rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants and enforceable by Indian courts (definition in the PHRA 1993).
- The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)** was adopted on **10 December 1948** (Human Rights Day). It is a non-binding declaration that inspired the binding **ICCPR** and **ICESCR (1966)**.

## Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

Created a three-tier machinery:

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **NHRC** | National-level watchdog, HQ New Delhi (set up 12 Oct 1993) |
| **SHRCs** | State Human Rights Commissions |
| **Human Rights Courts** | Speedy trial of offences arising from rights violations |

- NHRC is a **statutory, multi-member, recommendatory** body — it can inquire, summon, and recommend, but its findings are **not binding** and it has a **limited role over the armed forces**.

## PHRA (Amendment) Act, 2019

- **Chairperson**: earlier only a **former CJI**; now a former CJI **or a Judge of the Supreme Court**.
- **Term**: reduced from **5 years to 3 years** (chairperson and members), reappointment allowed.
- Added the chairpersons of the **NCBC, NCPCR and Chief Commissioner for PwD** as deemed members; allowed SHRC chairperson to be a former **High Court** Chief Justice or judge.
keyPoints: UDHR was adopted on 10 December 1948, marked as Human Rights Day; it is a non-binding declaration.
The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 created the NHRC, State Human Rights Commissions and Human Rights Courts.
NHRC is a statutory, recommendatory body (findings not binding) with a limited role over the armed forces.
PHRA (Amendment) Act 2019 cut the NHRC term from 5 to 3 years and let a sitting-type SC judge (not only a former CJI) be chairperson.
NHRC headquarters is in New Delhi; it was set up on 12 October 1993.
items.mnemonic: PHRA gives 'N-S-H' bodies: NHRC, SHRC, Human Rights Courts.
items.source: Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 & Amendment Act 2019 (nhrc.nic.in); UN — UDHR

items.title: Right to Information — Act 2005 and its amendments
items.body:
## RTI Act, 2005

- Enacted **15 June 2005**, in force from **12 October 2005**; replaced the Freedom of Information Act 2002. Flows from the Article 19(1)(a) right to know (*S.P. Gupta*, *Raj Narain*).
- Every public authority appoints a **Public Information Officer (PIO)**; reply due in **30 days** (48 hours if life/liberty is involved).
- Appeal ladder: **First Appellate Authority → Information Commission (CIC / SIC)**.
- **Section 8** lists exemptions (national security, cabinet papers, commercial confidence, personal information under 8(1)(j), etc.).

## RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019

- Earlier the Act **fixed** the term (5 years) and salaries of the CIC/ICs on par with Election Commissioners.
- The 2019 amendment let the **Central Government prescribe** their tenure, salaries and allowances by rules (tenure later set at **3 years**) — criticised as reducing their independence.

## DPDP Act, 2023 impact on RTI

- Section 44(3) of the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023** amended **Section 8(1)(j)** so that **all 'personal information' is exempt**, dropping the earlier public-interest/legislature proviso — seen as diluting transparency.
keyPoints: RTI Act was enacted on 15 June 2005 and came into force on 12 October 2005, replacing the 2002 Act.
A Public Information Officer must reply within 30 days (48 hours where life or liberty is at stake).
Appeals go from the First Appellate Authority to the Central/State Information Commission.
The RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 let the Centre fix the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners (earlier fixed at 5 years).
The DPDP Act 2023 amended RTI Section 8(1)(j) to exempt all personal information, widening the exemption.
items.source: RTI Act 2005 (rti.gov.in); RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 & DPDP Act 2023 (PRS Legislative Research)

items.title: Right to Education & Consumer Protection
items.body:
## Right to Education

- **Article 21A** (inserted by the **86th Amendment, 2002**) makes free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children **aged 6-14**.
- The **RTE Act 2009** (in force **1 April 2010**) operationalises it: **25% reservation** of entry-level seats in private unaided schools for EWS/disadvantaged children [s.12(1)(c)], no capitation fee, and norms for infrastructure and pupil-teacher ratio.
- The **2019 amendment** allowed states to end the automatic no-detention policy (regular exams in Classes 5 and 8).

## Consumer Protection Act, 2019

- Replaced the 1986 Act; in force **20 July 2020**. Recognises **six consumer rights** (safety, information, choice, to be heard, redressal, consumer education).
- Created the **Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)** to act against unfair trade practices and misleading ads (can order product recall, penalise endorsers).
- Added **product liability**, **e-commerce rules** and **mediation**.

### Three-tier redressal & pecuniary limits

| Forum | 2019 Act (original) | 2021 revised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| District Commission | up to ₹1 crore | up to ₹50 lakh |
| State Commission | ₹1-₹10 crore | ₹50 lakh-₹2 crore |
| National Commission (NCDRC) | above ₹10 crore | above ₹2 crore |
keyPoints: Article 21A (86th Amendment 2002) makes education a Fundamental Right for ages 6-14; the RTE Act 2009 took effect on 1 April 2010.
RTE Act reserves 25% of entry-level seats in private unaided schools for EWS/disadvantaged children.
The Consumer Protection Act 2019 replaced the 1986 Act and created the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA).
The Act recognises six consumer rights and introduced product liability and e-commerce rules.
Revised (2021) pecuniary limits: District up to ₹50 lakh, State ₹50 lakh-₹2 crore, National above ₹2 crore.
items.source: RTE Act 2009 (Ministry of Education); Consumer Protection Act 2019 & Jurisdiction Rules 2021 (Dept. of Consumer Affairs)

items.title: Rights of women — constitutional provisions & laws
items.body:
## Constitutional provisions

- **Art 15(3)** — enables special provisions for women and children.
- **Art 39(a)(d)** — equal livelihood and equal pay; **Art 42** — maternity relief; **Art 51A(e)** — duty to renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity.
- **National Commission for Women (NCW)** — statutory body under the **NCW Act 1990** (set up 1992); recommendatory.

## Key statutes

| Law | Thrust |
| --- | --- |
| **Dowry Prohibition Act 1961** | Bans giving/taking dowry |
| **PCPNDT Act 1994** | Bans prenatal sex determination |
| **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005** | Civil remedy — protection, residence, monetary orders via Protection Officers |
| **Sexual Harassment (POSH) Act 2013** | Codified the **Vishaka Guidelines (1997)**; mandates an **Internal Complaints Committee (ICC)** in workplaces with 10+ staff |
| **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013** | 'Nirbhaya Act' on the **Justice Verma Committee** report — added acid attack, stalking, voyeurism; widened rape definition |
| **Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017** | Raised paid leave **12 → 26 weeks** |
keyPoints: Article 15(3) is an enabling provision allowing special measures for women and children.
The National Commission for Women is a statutory body under the NCW Act 1990 (set up 1992).
The POSH Act 2013 codified the Vishaka (1997) guidelines and requires an Internal Complaints Committee in workplaces with 10+ employees.
The Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 (Nirbhaya Act) followed the Justice J.S. Verma Committee and added offences like acid attack and stalking.
The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 increased paid maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks.
items.source: Constitution of India; NCW Act 1990; PWDVA 2005; POSH Act 2013; Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013; Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017

items.title: Rights of the child — constitutional basis & laws
items.body:
## Constitutional basis

- **Art 21A** — right to education (6-14); **Art 24** — no child below 14 in factories/mines/hazardous work; **Art 39(e)(f)** — protection from abuse and healthy development; **Art 45** — early childhood care; **Art 51A(k)** — parental duty to provide education.
- **NCPCR** — statutory body under the **Commissions for Protection of Child Rights (CPCR) Act 2005**; monitors RTE, POCSO and JJ Act.

## Key statutes

| Law | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| **Juvenile Justice (Care & Protection) Act 2015** | Allows **16-18** year-olds to be tried as adults for **heinous** offences; created **JJ Boards** and **Child Welfare Committees** |
| **POCSO Act 2012** | **Gender-neutral**; protects all children under 18; Special Courts; 2019 amendment added death penalty for aggravated assault |
| **Child Labour (Amendment) Act 2016** | Bans employment below **14** in **all** occupations; **14-18 (adolescents)** barred from hazardous work |
keyPoints: Article 24 bars children below 14 from factories, mines and hazardous employment.
NCPCR is a statutory body under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act 2005.
The JJ Act 2015 permits 16-18 year-olds to be tried as adults for heinous offences and set up JJ Boards and Child Welfare Committees.
POCSO Act 2012 is gender-neutral and protects all children under 18; the 2019 amendment added the death penalty for aggravated assault.
The Child Labour (Amendment) Act 2016 bans all employment of children below 14 and hazardous work for adolescents 14-18.
items.source: Constitution of India; CPCR Act 2005; JJ Act 2015; POCSO Act 2012; Child Labour (Amendment) Act 2016

items.title: SC/ST, disability & other vulnerable groups
items.body:
## Scheduled Castes & Scheduled Tribes

- **Art 17** abolishes untouchability; **Art 46** directs promotion of SC/ST interests; **Art 335** on their claims in services; **Art 15(4)/16(4)** enable reservation; **Art 330/332** reserve legislative seats.
- **NCSC (Art 338)** and **NCST (Art 338A)** — bifurcated by the **89th Amendment 2003**; **NCBC (Art 338B)** added by the **102nd Amendment 2018**.
- **Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955** (untouchability) and the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989**; the **2018 amendment** (Section 18A) reversed the *Subhash Kashinath Mahajan* dilution to restore the bar on anticipatory bail.

## Persons with disabilities

- **RPwD Act 2016** (in force 19 Apr 2017) replaced the 1995 Act; raised recognised disabilities **7 → 21**; **4% reservation** in government jobs and **5%** in higher education; gives effect to the **UNCRPD** (India ratified 2007).

## Transgender persons & senior citizens

- **Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019** — followed **NALSA v Union of India (2014)** which recognised the third gender; set up the National Council for Transgender Persons.
- **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007** — makes maintenance of parents/senior citizens a legal duty.
keyPoints: Article 17 abolishes untouchability; the NCSC (Art 338) and NCST (Art 338A) were bifurcated by the 89th Amendment 2003.
The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 was strengthened by the 2018 amendment (Section 18A) after the Subhash Kashinath Mahajan ruling.
The RPwD Act 2016 raised recognised disabilities from 7 to 21 and gives 4% reservation in jobs and 5% in higher education.
The RPwD Act 2016 implements the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (ratified by India in 2007).
The Transgender Persons Act 2019 followed the NALSA (2014) judgment; the MWPSC Act 2007 makes maintenance of senior citizens a legal obligation.
items.source: Constitution of India; SC/ST (PoA) Act 1989 & Amendment 2018; RPwD Act 2016; Transgender Persons Act 2019; MWPSC Act 2007

items.title: International human rights conventions India follows
items.body:
## Major UN conventions

| Convention | Year adopted | India ratified | Subject |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **UDHR** | 1948 | (voted for) | Foundational declaration |
| **ICCPR / ICESCR** | 1966 | 1979 | Civil-political / economic-social rights |
| **CEDAW** | 1979 | 1993 | Discrimination against women |
| **CRC** | 1989 | 1992 | Rights of the child |
| **CRPD** | 2006 | 2007 | Persons with disabilities |

- Many domestic laws are the **enabling legislation** for these treaties — e.g. the **RPwD Act 2016** implements the **CRPD**, and child laws draw on the **CRC**.
- The **judiciary and PILs** (Vishaka, NALSA, RTE cases) and **NGOs** are key enforcers, often reading unratified international norms into Article 21.
keyPoints: CEDAW (1979) covers discrimination against women; India ratified it in 1993.
The Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC, 1989) was ratified by India in 1992.
The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD, 2006) was ratified by India in 2007.
Domestic laws such as the RPwD Act 2016 are enabling legislation for these UN conventions.
Indian courts read international human-rights norms into Article 21 through PILs (Vishaka, NALSA).
items.source: UN human rights treaties — OHCHR; Indian implementing statutes

items.title: PYQ Precision — Property, Fifth Schedule & UDHR
items.body:
## Right to Property

- **44th Amendment 1978** deleted Art 19(1)(f) & Art 31, ending property as a Fundamental Right.
- Now a **legal/constitutional right under Art 300A** — available to **any person** (not only citizens).

## Fifth Schedule & tribal land

- Governs administration of **Scheduled Areas & STs** (10 States); the Governor heads a **Tribes Advisory Council** and may modify/exclude laws.
- **Restricts/prohibits transfer of tribal land to non-tribals**; PESA 1996 extends panchayat powers here. Sixth Schedule = NE autonomous councils.

## UDHR in the Constitution

- UDHR (**10 Dec 1948**) values appear in the **Preamble, DPSP and Fundamental Duties** (besides Fundamental Rights).
- Binding covenants **ICCPR & ICESCR (1966)**, ratified by India in **1979**.

## Sub-classification of SCs

- In **2024 a 7-judge Supreme Court** bench held that **States CAN sub-classify Scheduled Castes** for reservation (overruling *E.V. Chinnaiah*, 2004).
keyPoints: 44th Amendment 1978 made property a legal right under Art 300A, available to any person.
Fifth Schedule restricts transfer of tribal land to non-tribals (Scheduled Areas, 10 States).
UDHR (1948) values reflected in the Preamble, DPSP and Fundamental Duties.
ICCPR & ICESCR (1966) were ratified by India in 1979.
In 2024 a 7-judge Supreme Court bench allowed States to sub-classify Scheduled Castes.
items.source: UPSC 2020/2021/2022 Prelims; Constitution Art 300A & Fifth Schedule; SC (2024) sub-classification
